title: Forward hum
purpose: Feel resonance move up and forward into your face and lips. The source presents this as part of lightening and brightening a voice.
instructions: Breathe in through your nose, then hum gently on a comfortable pitch. Notice where you feel the vibration.
Hum again, aiming the sound forward. See if you can make your lips tingle.
When that feels comfortable, keep smiling and move from the hum into a vowel: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo.
Then say short words that start with m, holding the m a little longer at first: meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

primary_cue.text: Aim the hum forward until your lips tingle.

cues.text: Aim the hum forward until your lips tingle.
Let a little air out through your nose just before you hum, like “hhhmmm”.
Imagine throwing your voice onto the ground in front of you.
Smile and start with a quiet hum, then slowly get a little louder until you feel a tingle on your lips.

practice_task.prompt_text: Hum forward, then say: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo — meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

check_questions.text: Where did you feel the vibration most?

dose_guidance.text: This activity gives no repetition count. Take your time and don't move on too fast. The NHS Fife progression page suggests short, frequent practice in general.

expected_observations: Vibration in the face, lips and nose; the lips may tingle.
Over time, noticing when resonance has “dropped” and bringing it back up.
common_misunderstandings: Pitch alone does not decide how a voice sounds. Where you feel resonance also matters.
Lighter does not mean quieter or whispery.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
adaptations: You can make up your own m-words.
You can stay on the hum and vowel steps for as long as you need.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt does not measure resonance automatically. Feedback comes from what you report and from listening back.
